🎧 Topic: Family Conflict: Curfew and Trust

🎧 Bấm phát để nghe hội thoại. Mèo sẽ xuất hiện ngay khi bạn nộp bài nha!

Listening Transcript

The yellow highlights show evidence for the correct answers. Review them after completing the test.

Study tip: Look for key details about the parents’ concerns, Trâm’s curfew, and the final compromise.

Click a word or select a phrase in the transcript. Then press “Dịch” to see its Vietnamese meaning.

Đức: Trâm, why do you look so upset? Did something happen at home?

Trâm: Yes. My parents won’t let me go to my best friend’s birthday party this Saturday. They say I spend too much time with my friends and not enough time studying.

Đức: That sounds frustrating. Have you tried explaining why the party matters to you?

Trâm: I did! But they keep saying my grades might get worse. My curfew is nine o’clock, so I would have to leave before the party even gets interesting.

Đức: Maybe they’re not trying to control you. They might just be worried about your safety and schoolwork.

Trâm: I understand that, but I’m sixteen now. I want them to trust me to make my own decisions. Whenever I disagree with them, they think I’m being disrespectful.

Đức: I think the problem is how you communicate. Instead of arguing, why don’t you show them you’re responsible?

Trâm: How? I’ve already promised to finish my homework before Saturday.

Đức: Then make a clear plan. Tell them where the party is, who will be there, and how you’ll get home. You could also agree to come home earlier than your friends.

Trâm: That’s actually a good idea. I’ll talk to them again tonight.

Đức: Later that evening…

Trâm: Mom and Dad, can we talk about Saturday again? I’ve finished my homework, and I’ll share the party address with you. Could I stay until ten thirty instead of nine?

Trâm: I also promise to keep my phone on and message you to let you know I’m safe.

Đức: Wait, I’m playing your dad now? Anyway, let’s say your parents agree to pick you up at ten thirty, provided you keep your promise.

Trâm: Really? That’s fair. I still wish I could stay until midnight, but I appreciate that they’re willing to compromise.

Đức: Exactly. Family conflicts don’t always mean someone is wrong. Sometimes, parents and teenagers simply have different concerns. Listening to each other and finding common ground can help both sides understand one another.

Trâm: I’ve learned that being independent also means being responsible. Thank you for listening!
